scenario: AITA for being home all day and refusing to cook for my mom? | I'm a female in my senior year of high school and I have a younger sister in grade 10. As most of you know, schools have been closed for a while now and won't reopen for at least another month. My dad gets to work from home, but my mom still has to go out to her office. My school just started online teaching, and we've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. However, my mom expects us to make dinner basically every night because "we're home all day". That really annoyed me because yeah "we're home all day" but we have school work to do. I got upset and asked her why doesn't she cook, since she always finishes work at 5 pm and her office is like 6 minutes from home. Well, once she got home today and saw there was no dinner prepared, she got pissed and started screaming at me how she's so ashamed of us and how we're useless. When I explained how yes we're home all day but doesn't mean we have the whole day off, she got even more mad and said that it doesn't take that long to cook. I refuted by "why don't you cook then?" For more context, my mom is an awful cook. She literally puts no effort into learning or looking up recipes. My dad is an excellent cook. He's tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, he would cook for us almost every day, even if he came home late from work (he has a high demanding job so his hours range but he's home 6 pm the EARLIEST, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm. + 30-40 minutes one way commuting). And what does he come home to? Either a low effort flavourless meal from my mom, or my mom sitting on her ass watching TV and asking him what's he's gonna make for dinner. So my dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast-food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if us girls are hungry and offers to cook something for us to eat because he's worried that our mom didn't make us a proper meal. I'm a good cook too (self taught), and I try to help out if I don't have too much homework to do. I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. Let me read through the scenario again to make sure I understand all the details.

So, there's a high school senior girl and her younger sister who are both at home because schools are closed. Their dad works from home, but their mom still goes to her office. The schools have started online teaching, and they have a lot of assignments to do. The mom expects them to cook dinner every night because they're home all day. The girl is annoyed because even though they're home, they have schoolwork to do. She gets upset and asks her mom why she doesn't cook since she finishes work at 5 pm and her office is only 6 minutes away. The mom gets angry and starts yelling at them, saying she's ashamed and they're useless. The girl explains that being home all day doesn't mean they have the whole day off, and the mom says cooking doesn't take that long. The girl retorts by asking why the mom doesn't cook then.

From the context, the mom is an awful cook and doesn't put effort into learning or looking up recipes. The dad is an excellent cook and used to cook almost every day, even when he came home late from work. He's tried to teach the mom, but she refuses. The dad often ends up eating fast food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be ready. He also checks if the girls are hungry and offers to cook for them. The girl is a good cook too and has been helping out with cooking and baking treats during the first few weeks before online school started. The dad does almost all the chores, while the mom spends her time watching TV.

The question is whether the girl is AITA (asking if it's acceptable) for not cooking dinner today and telling her mom not to expect dinner every time she comes home. The dad ended up cooking in the end.

Alright, so I need to evaluate whether the girl's action is morally acceptable or not. Let's break this down.

First, the mom expects the girls to cook dinner every night because they're home all day. However, the girls have schoolwork to do, which is a valid responsibility. The mom's expectation seems unreasonable because the girls are also juggling their education. The mom, on the other hand, finishes work at 5 pm and has a short commute, so she has more time to cook if she wanted to.

The mom is an awful cook and doesn't make an effort to improve. She relies on the dad to cook, who already has a demanding job and long hours. The dad is forced to cook late at night, which is inconvenient and adds to his stress. The girl is also a good cook and has been helping out, but she has her own responsibilities with schoolwork.

The girl's frustration is understandable. She's being asked to take on an additional responsibility without consideration for her own workload. When she confronts her mom, it escalates into an argument where the mom gets angry and criticizes the girls. The girl stands her ground by asking why the mom doesn't cook, which is a fair point given the mom's lack of effort.

The girl's decision not to cook dinner today and to set boundaries with her mom seems justified. She's asserting her own responsibilities and pushing back against an unfair expectation. The dad ended up cooking, which is a relief, but the girl's action doesn't seem morally wrong. She's advocating for herself and her sister's time and effort.

However, it's important to consider the communication style. The girl got upset and confronted her mom, which led to an argument. While her frustration is valid, the way she expressed it might have contributed to the conflict. Effective communication could have helped de-escalate the situation, but her main point about the unfair expectation is still valid.

In conclusion, the girl's action of not cooking dinner and setting boundaries with her mom is morally acceptable because she's balancing her responsibilities and standing up for herself against an unreasonable demand. The mom's refusal to take responsibility for cooking and her criticism of the girls are the problematic aspects here.
